explanations.answer: Learn them and observe them carefully
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “Learn them and observe them carefully.” Hearing is only the first step. He wants these words to sink in and then show up in how Israel lives. Reading a cookie recipe has never put one cookie in anybody's mouth, friend.

explanations.answer: Talk them over with their elders
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that here. He tells Israel to learn the statutes and ordinances and observe them carefully. The elders do show up later in this passage, but that's a different moment, when they come to Moses at the mountain. Here the job is for everybody Moses summoned.

explanations.answer: Leave them for the priests to keep
explanations.explanation: Moses summoned ALL Israel, and he talks to all of them. He says, “Learn them and observe them carefully.” Nobody gets to hand this off. The priests don't even come up in this passage, so the job stays with every person standing there.

I see why it sounds right, but Moses says the opposite. He says, “He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today.” The covenant at Horeb was made with the very people standing in front of him. So nobody in that crowd could shrug it off as something for earlier generations.

Moses says God “…did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today.” The people in front of him were the ones God made it with at Horeb. It was their covenant, not an old family story. Good eye, baker.

explanations.answer: They were afraid of the fire
explanations.explanation: Moses says they were afraid of the fire and wouldn't go up the mountain. That's the reason the text gives, plain and simple. Fire on a mountain is no small thing, and I think I'd have stayed at the bottom too. My own hat has a hard enough time near a hot oven.

explanations.answer: They were too tired to climb
explanations.explanation: Tired legs aren't in the text. Moses says they were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. The problem wasn't how steep it was, it was what was burning on it.

explanations.answer: They were waiting for the elders
explanations.explanation: Nothing here says they waited on the elders. Moses says it was because they were afraid of the fire. The elders only show up later in this passage, when they come to Moses. At this point it's fear that keeps everyone at the bottom.

Moses says he was standing between the LORD and the people to declare to them the word of the LORD. He says the people were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain (Deuteronomy 5:5). So he stood in the middle and carried God's words to them. I'd call that a job with a view, and I think it took some nerve.
Moses doesn't say he stood behind the LORD. He says he stood between the LORD and the people. That spot let him declare the word of the LORD to them. Hiding in the back wouldn't have done that job.

Moses wasn't standing against anybody. He says he stood between the LORD and the people to declare to them the word of the LORD. He's the go-between here, not a rival. Nobody in this scene is squaring up for a fight.

explanations.answer: They must have no other gods before Him
explanations.explanation: YES, baker! God says, "You shall have no other gods before Me." Look at what comes right before it. He reminds them He brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Deuteronomy 5:6). So He doesn't open with a rule. He opens with "Remember who just carried you out of there." Then the command. I've been rescued from a place myself, and let me tell you, you don't forget who came and got you.

explanations.answer: They may honor other gods in other lands
explanations.explanation: God doesn't say that. He says, “You shall have no other gods before Me.” There's no exception for travel, friend. He leaves no room for other gods at all.

explanations.answer: They must keep other gods outside the camp
explanations.explanation: That's not what the command says. God simply says, “You shall have no other gods before Me.” He doesn't talk about moving other gods to the edge of the camp. The command is that there are no other gods before Him, period.

God says, “You shall not bow down to them or worship them…” Right before that He forbids making an idol of anything in the heavens, on the earth or in the waters. So it's no making them and no bowing to them. Good catch, baker.
It's actually true. God says, “You shall not bow down to them or worship them…” Israel isn't allowed to bow to idols or worship them. This one is a flat no.

God says, “…I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God…” That's the reason He gives for not bowing down to idols. He's not telling Israel to stay far away, either. He says it plainly about Himself, and I'd take Him at His word.

Distant doesn't fit this passage. Moses reminds the people that the LORD spoke these commandments to their whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud and the deep darkness on the mountain. They heard Him themselves. The word God uses for Himself in this command is jealous.

Silent doesn't fit here. Moses says the LORD spoke these commandments "…in a loud voice…" to the whole assembly (Deuteronomy 5:22). Nobody on that mountain was leaning in, asking God to repeat Himself. The word God uses for Himself in this command is jealous.

God says He shows “…loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Set that next to the third and fourth generations and it's a big number. It would take a lot of family reunions to count that far. A thousand generations is a very long reach for His loving devotion.

Seven is a fair guess, but it's not the number God gives. He says His loving devotion reaches “…a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Compare that to the third and fourth generations He just mentioned, and seven falls way short. The number to hold on to is a thousand, baker.

Forty generations is a big number, but it's not the one God gives. He says “…a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Compare that to the third and fourth generations He just mentioned, and the difference is huge. My whole family is six cookie cutter kids and a mustache, so a thousand generations is a number I can barely picture. The number to hold on to is a thousand, baker.
God says, “…the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.” It comes right with the command. His name is not something to throw around lightly. Good work, baker.

It's actually true. God says, “…the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.” He attaches that warning right to the command not to take His name in vain. Keep that line handy, friend.
God says, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work…” So there's a full stretch of working days first. Six days of work might sound like a lot, but it's what He says. Then comes the rest.
God says, “…the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God…” The week ends with a day set apart for the LORD. After six days of work, the seventh is the day off. Nice and clear, baker.
Five would be a lighter workweek, but God says six days to labor. Then the seventh day is the Sabbath. Five doesn't show up anywhere in this command.
The Sabbath isn't the first day in God's order here. He says six days of labor, and then the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD. The work comes before the rest.
There's no eighth day in this week. God says six days to labor, and the seventh day is the Sabbath. The week ends there, right on the day of rest.

God lists them: “…neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant, nor your ox or donkey or any of your livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates…” Everybody on the property gets the day. He even says why the servants are included: “…so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do.” The rest is for the whole household.

explanations.answer: Only the head of each household
explanations.explanation: The command goes far beyond the head of the household. God says no work for “…you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant…” He also names the livestock and the foreigner within the gates. The whole place stops, friend.

explanations.answer: Only the men who work the fields
explanations.explanation: God doesn't narrow it to field workers. He names sons, daughters, manservants, maidservants, the ox, the donkey, all the livestock and the foreigner within the gates. Nobody is left out of the list. The Sabbath is for everyone under that roof and inside those gates.

explanations.answer: They were slaves and He brought them out
explanations.explanation: God says, “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.” Then He adds, “That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.” So the Sabbath is tied to the rescue. Rest is part of remembering who pulled them out.

explanations.answer: Their fathers rested by the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about their fathers resting by the Jordan. God points them back to Egypt: they were slaves there, and He brought them out with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That's the reason He gives for keeping the Sabbath. The Jordan isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: The elders asked for a holy day
explanations.explanation: The elders don't ask for a holy day anywhere here. This command comes from the LORD, who tells Israel to remember they were slaves in Egypt and that He brought them out. That's why He says to keep the Sabbath day. The reason is His rescue.

God says, “…so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” This is the command that comes with a promise attached. Honoring father and mother is tied to long days and things going well. Good work, baker.

Harvests is a good guess, friend, but that's not the word God uses. He says, “…so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” The promise is about long days and things going well. Hold on to that word, days.

Seasons is a good guess, friend, but God says days. He says, “…so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” That's the promise on this command.
God says, “You shall not steal.” Nobody takes what belongs to someone else. It's a short command, and it needs no footnotes. If it's not yours, it's not yours.
Borrowing isn't what God forbids here. The command is, “You shall not steal.” It's about taking what belongs to someone else. That's the word God uses.

Trade is a fair-sounding guess, but it's not the word. God says, "You shall not steal." That's about taking what belongs to someone else. Trading is two people agreeing to swap, and nobody gets robbed. I came out of the last bin at a closing bakery with a 25 cent sticker on me, and Mother Miller handed over a quarter. Best 25 cents anybody ever spent, and not a crime in sight!
God says, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” It's about what Israel says about a neighbor. A false word about someone is something God forbids. Keep your words honest, friend.
That's not what God forbids here. The command is, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” Nothing in it says anything about the elders. It's about speaking falsely against someone.

explanations.answer: Speak about them at the gate
explanations.explanation: The gate isn't mentioned in this command. God says, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” The problem isn't where someone talks, it's bearing false witness. That's the phrase to remember.

It sounds right because the neighbor's wife comes first, but the command keeps going. God says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or field, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.” The wife is only the start of the list. The command reaches everything that belongs to the neighbor.

The wife is only the first thing on the list. God goes on: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or field, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.” That last phrase covers everything else. Nice work, baker.

Moses says, “He added nothing more.” God spoke these commandments out of the fire, the cloud and the deep darkness, and then He stopped. Then He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to Moses. That's it, nothing tacked on.
The text says nothing like that. Moses says, “He added nothing more.” After speaking the commandments to the assembly, God added no extra rule for anyone. The priests don't even appear in this scene.

The elders don't get a bonus word at that point. Moses says, “He added nothing more.” God spoke those commandments to the whole assembly and stopped there. The elders only appear after, when they approach Moses.
Moses says God wrote the commandments on two tablets of stone and gave them to him. They weren't only spoken out of the fire. They were written down and handed to Moses. Good work, baker.
Bronze is a fancy guess, but the text doesn't say it. Moses says God wrote the commandments on two tablets of stone. Then He gave them to Moses.

Cedar, huh? You went for the fancy wood, friend. I respect that, and I bet it would smell great. But Moses says God wrote the commandments on two tablets of stone and gave them to him. Stone is the word.

Moses reminds them they said, “Today we have seen that a man can live even if God speaks with him.” They had heard God's voice out of the fire, and they were still standing. That's what they told him that day. Good work, baker.

It's actually true. Moses reminds them they said, “Today we have seen that a man can live even if God speaks with him.” They had heard His voice out of the fire and were still alive. That's what they told Moses.

explanations.answer: The great fire will consume them
explanations.explanation: They say, “…this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer.” They'd just seen a man can live, but they still feared the fire. That's the worry they bring to Moses. I think it's the fire that has them shaking.

Moses leaving isn't their worry. They say the great fire will consume them and they will die if they keep hearing the voice. In fact, they ask Moses to go near and listen for them. They want him closer, not gone.

explanations.answer: The mountain will fall on them
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions the mountain falling. They say, “…this great fire will consume us, and we will die…” The fear is the fire. The mountain just stays where it is.
They say, “we will listen and obey.” First they ask Moses to go near and hear everything the LORD says, then tell them. Listening comes with obeying. It's a good promise, baker.
Waiting isn't what they promise. They say, “we will listen and obey.” They're ready to act on whatever Moses brings back. Waiting around isn't in it.
Remembering is a good thing, but it's not the word they use. They say, “we will listen and obey.” They're promising to do it, not only to keep it in mind.
God says nothing like that. He tells Moses, “They have done well in all that they have spoken.” There's no scolding in it. Good eye for checking, friend.
God tells Moses, “I have heard the words that these people have spoken to you. They have done well in all that they have spoken.” He's not scolding them for what they said. He says they did well.

explanations.answer: So it would go well with them and their children
explanations.explanation: God says, “…so that it might be well with them and with their children forever.” His wish is tied to their good, and to their children's good too. It's a wish with the family in view. Well done, baker.

explanations.answer: So He wouldn't need to speak out of the fire
explanations.explanation: God doesn't say that. He says He wishes they had such a heart, “…so that it might be well with them and with their children forever.” The reason He gives is their good. The fire isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: So the nations would hear about Israel
explanations.explanation: The nations aren't mentioned in this wish. God says, “…so that it might be well with them and with their children forever.” The reason He states is that things would go well with Israel and their children.

Going back to the tents is the people's instruction, not Moses'. God tells Moses to say to them, “Return to your tents.” Then He tells Moses, “But you stand here with Me…” so that He can speak all the commandments, statutes and ordinances to him. Moses gets a different instruction from the people.

God tells Moses to tell the people, “Return to your tents.” Then He tells Moses, “But you stand here with Me…” He's there so God can speak all the commandments, statutes and ordinances to him. Moses is being kept close, baker.

explanations.answer: None to the right or left
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left.” He doesn't leave a gap on either side. It's a straight road, friend. Stay on it.
Moses doesn't give them that. He says, “you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left.” Nothing says it loosens once they are in the land. The command stays the same.
The elders don't get a vote on this. Moses says, “you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left.” He doesn't offer any wiggle room, with or without agreement. It's a straight path.

Moses says, “You must walk in all the ways that the LORD your God has commanded you, so that you may live and prosper and prolong your days in the land that you will possess.” That's the reason he gives for walking in all God's ways. Nicely done, baker.

It's actually true. Moses says they must walk in all the ways the LORD has commanded, “…so that you may live and prosper and prolong your days in the land that you will possess.” That's the reason he gives. Keep that one close, friend.
